This analysis was followed by a Riks analysis of the tank where the atmospheric load was applied explicitly, and the buckling load was computed. The load is applied, step by step, until the structure buckles, the Riks method can capture post-buckling response as well. A ‘pre-existing defect’, computed via the eigenvalue analysis, was applied to the model to initiate buckling. The load proportionality factor (LPF) at the point of buckling, output from the results when multiplied by the applied pressure, yielded a buckling load of 11.7 times that of atmospheric pressure, confirming the result of the eigen-buckling analysis. This is deemed to be sufficient structural margin. If there is a need for more margin, then thickness of the tank can be increased and/or the thickness of the flange in the mid-section can be increased, stiffening the area of the tank most likely to buckle. This model was to be re-run with more updated properties when available. Cylindrical (Phase 1) composite tank Inner Tank thermo-structural Analysis: An FE model of the inner tank was set up- as seen in Figure 8. Composite material properties for the tank (material: Teijin IMS65-Q183) are unavailable since the materials test program had just commenced. At the termination of the program, only room temperature properties were tested, but not at cryogenic temperatures. For a reasonably accurate analysis, cryogenic properties of the material are also required. Hence, properties of a similar/equivalent composite i.e. a carbon -epoxy unidirectional tape (Toray T800-epoxy) were taken from literature [2], where both room temperature and cryogenic temperatures were available. Li et. al. [2]. tested, computed and validated composite properties for carbon fiber epoxy system at ambient and cryogenic temperatures. The FE model consists of the tank, the boss (i.e. flange, bolt, sealing, cushion and tubes etc.). A detailed boss design was created, and used in this model. The loading in the FE model has 3 parts to it: (i) compression of the seal and composite tank due to bolt loads, (ii) thermal stresses due to cool down, and (iii) stresses in the tank due to internal pressure. It was expected that stresses in the area of the tank in contact with the boss will be affected by bolt load and also by the cooldown- hence the need to model all the loads in a single model. Temperature profiles (at equilibrium) were used to simulate the cooling process. The model has contact enforced between the upper bulkhead and the seal, the seal and the composite tank, and between the tank and the cushion below it. The composite tank is modeled at ply-level detail where individual ply directions are defined.
